pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–11 years

- **Topic:** Drawing Particle Diagrams

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter' — Particle model):** The differences in arrangements, in motion and in closeness of particles explaining changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles. (Bridged down from KS2 states work; formal particle model is KS3.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS1-4 / 5-PS1-1):** [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS1-4]; [curriculum wording omitted; reference 5-PS1-1]. Examples of models include drawing and diagrams.

- **Operational details:** This is a REPRESENTATIONAL node — the child learns to DRAW and READ the canonical dot diagram: solids (particles close, in a regular pattern, vibrating in place), liquids (close, irregular, sliding past each other), gases (far apart, fast, random). The diagram is a tool for reasoning: from it the child explains fixed shape (solids), flow (liquids), and compressibility (gas gaps). Two conventions must be taught precisely: (1) the PARTICLES themselves do not change size, colour or state — only their spacing, pattern and motion change; (2) the space between gas particles is EMPTY (nothing there), not air. Introduce arrangement first (a static snapshot), then motion (arrows / animation). Have pupils sketch the before/after of a state change (e.g. melting) and annotate what changed.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional). The child draws correct arrangement AND indicates motion for each state, and uses the diagram to explain at least one observable property (shape, flow, or compressibility) — without attributing macroscopic properties to individual particles.
bestPractices: Teach arrangement (a snapshot) before motion, then add movement with arrows or animation so both are represented.
Anchor every diagram to an observable property it explains (fixed shape, flow, compressibility) so drawing is reasoning, not decoration.
Insist particles keep the same size/identity across states — only spacing, pattern and motion change.
Establish that the gaps between gas particles are empty, not filled with air or 'nothing visible'.
Have pupils draw before/after a state change and annotate what changed, linking to heating/cooling.
keyRepresentations: The canonical solid/liquid/gas dot diagram (arrangement + spacing)
Motion arrows or animation showing vibrate-in-place vs slide vs fly-free
A before/after pair for a state change (e.g. melting) with annotation
Same-particle overlay proving the particles are identical across states
commonMisconceptions: Particles themselves expand, melt, change colour or change state (attributing macroscopic properties to particles).
The space between particles is filled with air/gas rather than being empty.
Gas particles sit only at the bottom of a container.
Particle size or number changes between states, rather than only spacing and motion.
Solids' particles are completely still (they actually vibrate in place).

learn.summary: Learners aged 7–11 learn to draw and read the canonical particle (dot) diagrams for solids (particles close, in a regular pattern, vibrating in place), liquids (close, irregularly arranged, sliding past each other), and gases (far apart, moving fast in random directions). The diagram is a reasoning tool: from it learners explain fixed shape, flow, and compressibility. Two conventions must be taught precisely — (1) the particles themselves do not change size, colour, number or state across states; only spacing, pattern and motion change; and (2) the space between gas particles is empty, not filled with air. Teach a static arrangement snapshot first, then add motion. Learners sketch before/after a state change (e.g. melting) and annotate what changed, linking to heating and cooling.

activities.title: Particle diagram lab: place, play, and test
feedback: If particles overlap, prompt the learner to redraw them as separate dots that do not overlap; if a gas clumps at the bottom of the container, prompt: gas particles fill the whole space and don't pile up — spread them out randomly throughout the box.
If the gas gaps are shaded or filled, ask 'what IS the gas?' — the particles ARE the gas (if the gas is air, the particles are the air); between them is empty space. Remove the fill.
If dots change size between states, remind: same object, same particles — only spacing and arrangement change. Redraw keeping every dot identical in size across all three states.

After the squash test, ask the learner to say, in their own words, why the gas compressed much more than the solid or liquid (its particles have empty gaps to close, while the others are already close-packed).
activities.rationale: An interactive model where arrangement is set, motion is played, and consequences (holding shape, flowing, compressing) are observed turns a static drawing convention into reasoning. A same-particle counter and a compression test make conservation and compressibility concrete. These are concrete, optional interaction examples that make the mechanism visible, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': differences in arrangement, motion and closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles
NGSS MS-PS1-4: develop a model (incl drawings/diagrams) predicting changes in particle motion, temperature and state; 5-PS1-1 matter is particles too small to see
learnerActions: Choose a state and place particles accordingly: a solid in neat regular rows, a liquid close together but disordered, a gas spread far apart.

Add motion to the arrangement — show solid particles vibrating in place without leaving their spots, liquid particles sliding and tumbling over each other, and gas particles scattering and bouncing off the walls.

Run a 'squash the container' test and observe compression qualitatively: the gas visibly compresses as its empty gaps get smaller, while the solid and liquid show very little change (they are hard to compress, not perfectly incompressible).
Watch a running count of particles stay the same across every state, and keep every dot the same size when switching states, to show number and size are conserved.

Model melting: take the solid and show its particles loosening out of the regular pattern into a disordered arrangement and speeding up — staying close together (still touching, not moving far apart; only a small spacing change) and remaining the same particles — then annotate what changed.
activities.intendedInsight: A particle diagram becomes a working model only when it both shows arrangement and moves: from it a learner can explain why solids keep shape, liquids flow, and gases can be squashed, and why heating to melt rearranges and speeds up particles without changing the particles themselves.

activities.title: Canonical reference and hand-drawing on paper
feedback: Check hand-drawn work for the three tells: same-size dots throughout, empty gas gaps, and motion marks on every state (solids vibrate, liquids slide, gases fly).
If a learner can label a given diagram but hesitates to draw one, prompt them to generate a fresh liquid diagram from scratch rather than copy.
A reference is a memory anchor; being static it cannot show motion or let the learner test compressibility — pair it with drawing and a dynamic model to cover those.
activities.rationale: A labelled reference with 'what this explains' notes is a convention guide and memory anchor, and connecting each diagram to the property it explains instantiates the curriculum point that arrangement/motion/closeness explain state, shape and density. Hand-drawing on paper supports independent production rather than recognition. The static reference's limit (no motion, no compressibility test) is stated so it is used as a companion, not a substitute.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Physics 'Matter/Particle model': differences in arrangement, motion and closeness of particles explain changes of state, shape and density; atoms and molecules as particles
learnerActions: Study a reference of the three canonical diagrams, each labelled with its arrangement, spacing and motion.
For each diagram, read the accompanying 'what this explains' note (fixed shape, flow, or compressibility) and connect the picture to the property.
Draw all three diagrams by hand on paper, keeping dots the same size and leaving gas gaps empty, then label arrangement and motion for each.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent recall and hand-production of the canonical conventions anchors the representation so it can be used without a prompt; a reference supports memory but the learner must still produce the diagrams independently.

activities.title: Read it and draw it: two-way check
feedback: If liquid particles are drawn far apart like a gas: liquids barely compress and don't spread out to fill a whole jar the way a gas does, so particles must still be touching — just disordered. Redraw touching-but-random.
If dots change size for different states: only spacing and arrangement change; keep every dot identical in size.
If gas gaps are filled: the particles ARE the gas; between them is nothing (empty space).
If motion is missing or only on one state: add motion to all three — solids vibrate in place, liquids slide, gases fly; none are truly still.

On the melting question, confirm: the dots stay the same size and number, while the regular pattern becomes disordered and the particles speed up, with only a small change in spacing — they do not fly far apart (that would be becoming a gas).
activities.rationale: Assessing both reading and generating discriminates genuine understanding: a learner who labels a textbook picture but draws liquid particles far apart, resizes dots, or fills gas gaps reveals the representation isn't yet carrying meaning. Probing prompts surface the two priority conventions (conserved particles, empty gaps).
sourceClaims: Students commonly attribute macroscopic properties to particles and imagine air/matter between particles; particles keep identity while spacing/motion change
learnerActions: Point to which of two given diagrams (dots spread far apart vs dots packed in a regular grid) is the gas and which is the solid, and explain the decision by spacing and arrangement.
On a blank box, draw the particles for a liquid — close together and touching but irregularly arranged — and add marks showing them sliding and flowing past each other.

Answer probing questions: In your liquid drawing, are the particles touching or apart, and how does that explain why water is very hard to squash? What's in the space between gas particles, and how do you know? When your solid melts, which parts of the picture change and which stay the same — do the dots themselves (their size and number) change, or is it the arrangement and motion that change while spacing changes only a little?
Critique a flawed example — 'someone drew big dots for gas and small dots for ice' — and say what you'd tell them.
activities.intendedInsight: Translating both ways — reading a given diagram AND generating a new one — catches errors a single direction hides, confirming the representation carries the meaning rather than being memorised.

constraints: The canonical curriculum representation is the 2D dot diagram; a 3D particle box can convey real spatial packing but adds interpretation load, so use it only as an optional extension, not the core drawing target.

Dialogue or in-role discussion alone does not let a learner produce or manipulate the diagram; the representational skill requires drawing/placing and reading. Discussion can still support reasoning around the diagram.
A static reference supports memory and convention but cannot show motion or let the learner test compressibility; pair it with hand-drawing and a dynamic model.
Recognition or labelling of a provided diagram does not demonstrate independent construction; always include a generate-from-blank task.
Teach arrangement (a snapshot) before motion, then add movement, so both aspects are represented.
Two conventions must be enforced: particles keep the same size, identity and number across states (only spacing, pattern and motion change); and the space between gas particles is empty, not air.
Anchor every diagram to an observable property it explains (fixed shape, flow, compressibility) so drawing is reasoning, not decoration.
Solids' particles vibrate in place — they are not completely still; gas particles fill the whole container and do not sit only at the bottom.

Melting (solid→liquid) keeps particles close/touching while changing a regular pattern to a disordered one and speeding them up, with only a small spacing change; do not depict particles moving far apart on melting (that depicts becoming a gas).
Keep the compression comparison qualitative: the gas visibly compresses while solids and liquids change very little; do not state solids/liquids are perfectly incompressible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The pedagogy note references 'energy changes involved' during a state change (one evidence statement); for ages 7–11 this is kept qualitative (heating speeds up and rearranges particles). Depth of energy treatment should be reviewed against the intended standard tier.

The source claim about learners attributing macroscopic properties to particles and imagining matter between particles is marked unverified in the row; treat the misconception framing as research-informed, not confirmed, and do not assert efficacy of any specific remedy.

The compression claim is kept qualitative: the gas visibly compresses while solids/liquids change little; avoid implying solids/liquids are perfectly incompressible, as the effect depends on scale/representation.

The original melting probe framed the change as 'the dots, the spacing, or both?'; because the particles (dots) do not change on melting, this was reworded so no learner-facing text implies the dots change or that particles spread far apart — only arrangement and motion change, with a small spacing change for most substances.

probeDeeper: In your liquid drawing, are the particles touching or apart? How does that explain why you can't squash water?
What's in the space between the gas particles — and how do you know?
If I heated your solid until it melted, what changes in the picture — the dots, the spacing, or both?
Someone drew big dots for gas and small dots for ice. What would you tell them?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the widely-spaced dots as gas and the packed regular grid as solid, justified by SPACING and ARRANGEMENT. Then draws a liquid as particles still close together (touching) but irregularly arranged, with movement marks showing them sliding/flowing past each other — not a neat grid (solid) and not far apart (gas). Same-size dots throughout; nothing drawn in the gaps.

errorPatterns.pattern: draws the particles themselves changing size — bigger for gas, smaller for solid ('they spread out AND get bigger')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Same object, same particles — only the SPACING and arrangement change. Have them redraw keeping every dot identical in size across all three states.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: gas dots drawn larger than solid dots; conflates particle size with spacing

errorPatterns.pattern: fills the gaps between gas particles with something ('there's air in between')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what IS the gas?' — the particles ARE the air; between them is nothing (empty space). Erase the fill.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: shades or dots the space between particles in the gas box

errorPatterns.pattern: draws liquid particles spaced far apart like a gas, not close like a solid
errorPatterns.nextMove: Liquids barely compress and don't shrink to fill a jar — so particles must still be touching, just disordered. Redraw touching-but-random.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: liquid box looks like the gas box, just fewer dots

errorPatterns.pattern: draws a solid's particles as perfectly still but forgets gas/liquid particles move (or vice versa)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Add motion to all three: solids VIBRATE in place, liquids slide, gases fly — none are truly still. Annotate each with its motion.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: no movement marks at all, or movement only on one state; solid dots shown with no vibration

responseLevels.gap: Mislabels the diagrams or can't justify by spacing; drawing shows size-changing dots, filled gaps, or liquid-as-gas.
responseLevels.full: Reads any state diagram by spacing+arrangement AND generates a correct liquid (close, disordered, sliding) with same-size dots, empty gaps, and state-appropriate motion — and uses the picture to explain a property (e.g. incompressibility) or a state change.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws arrangement/spacing correctly for the three states but omits or muddles movement, or can label a given diagram yet hesitates when generating one — the representation is read, not yet fluently produced.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Show the child a particle diagram of a gas (a few dots spread far apart in a box) and one of a solid (dots packed in a regular grid). First: 'Point to the gas and the solid — how did you decide?' Then hand them a blank box and say: 'Now YOU draw the particles for a liquid, and add little marks to show how they're moving.' Watch both the reading and the drawing.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Translating BOTH ways — reading a given diagram and generating a new one — catches errors a single direction hides. A child who can label a textbook picture but draws liquid particles far apart, or shrinks/grows the dots for state, or fills the gas gaps with 'air', reveals the representation isn't yet carrying the meaning.
